newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana to help bourse by sell-offs, ending fx curbs.
newsitem.headline: Ghana to help bourse by sell-offs, ending fx curbs.

text.p: Ghana is considering privatising more companies and relaxing remaining foreign exchange controls as a way of reinvigorating its flagging stock market.

"We will examine the divestiture policy, to see if some sell-offs could be done through the exchange," said Deputy Finance Minister Victor Selormey during a visit to the Ghana Stock Exchange on Wednesday.

Selormey, addressing council members' concern at declining investor interest in the Exchange, said new bills would soon be put before parliament to replace the "old and obsolete Exchange Control Act", and to change securities regulation.
He gave no details. In recent years the foreign exchange regime has been liberalised, to make the cedi's exchange rate more market-driven.
Turnover on the stock exchange fell to 35.75 million shares in 1996 from 55.84 million in 1995, and activity has stagnated this year.

The middle of the year is traditionally quiet because of holidays, while some investors hold back ahead of interim company results, but volume has struggled to reach 200,000 shares in recent thrice-weekly sessions.
One problem has been the competition from attractive rates of 40 to 45 percent available on treasury bills.

Selormey said he did not see "why interest rates should go up further in the foreseeable future", but added that attempts to cut interest rates would backfire if the economic fundamentals were not put right.
Inflation in April, the last month for which figures are available, stood at 29.1 percent. The government aims to reduce it to 15 percent by end-year with the help of high interest rates.
Selormey also said the stock market would be modernised and new technology introduced, with the aim of making it the financial hub of West Africa.
Yeboa Amoa, the Exchange's managing director, told the minister that one of the main challenges facing the local bourse was a planned regional stock exchange in Abidjan, Ivory Coast.

This exchange, which would serve the countries of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA) -- Benin, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Bissau, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo -- was supposed to have been in operation by mid-1997, and is now planned for the end of this year.
